sentences.text: Palaeocarcharodon is also known as the pygmy white shark, and the genus currently contains only one valid species, P. orientalis.
This animal belongs to the class Chondrichthyes and is classified within the family Cretoxyrhinidae.
Its teeth were triangular and compressed, featuring irregular serrations with serrate lateral cusplets, and could reach a length of about 3 to 6 centimeters.
Some teeth found in Volgograd, Russia, lack serrations and are classified as Palaeocarcharodon cf. orientalis.
The exact size of Palaeocarcharodon is uncertain, though it is estimated to have been comparable in size to mako sharks or modern great white sharks.
Fossil evidence for this shark consists of a few possible vertebrae and several teeth.
Fossils of Palaeocarcharodon have been found in the Americas, Asia, Russia, North Africa, and Europe.
The genus Palaeocarcharodon was named by Casier in 1960, while Sinzow originally named the species Carcharodon orientalis in 1899.
The type species of the genus is Carcharodon orientalis.
Palaeocarcharodon landanensis has been proposed as a synonym of Carcharodon orientalis.
The Paleobiology Database lists the parent group of Palaeocarcharodon as Otodontidae.
Palaeocarcharodon lived between 61.7 and 55.8 million years ago during the Middle Paleocene and Early Eocene.
The time range for Palaeocarcharodon is recorded as the Danian to Priabonian stages, from 66 to 33.9 million years ago.

The classification of Palaeocarcharodon remains a subject of debate among researchers. In 2013, some researchers suggested that P. landanensis is a senior synonym of P. orientalis, though this is still debated. While some theories placed Palaeocarcharodon in the family Otodontidae, recent papers generally classify it in Cretoxyrhinidae.
